source.title: Dynamical Isometry and a Mean Field Theory of RNNs: Gating Enables Signal Propagation in Recurrent Neural Networks
source.authors: Min-Min Chen; Jeffrey Pennington; S. Schoenholz

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, but its title is “Dynamical Isometry and a Mean Field Theory of RNNs: Gating Enables Signal Propagation in Recurrent Neural Networks,” rather than the listed title for arXiv:1806.05393.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how initialization affects training speed and trainability in recurrent networks, extending initialization findings to a new architecture and sequence task.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training outcomes for its own RNN experiments. The cited results from other studies are not rows. Figure 2 reports training accuracy and theoretical timescales, but the plotted values are not described numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The vanilla tanh RNN experiments test V4's initialization–trainability relationship in a recurrent setting: critical initialization improves convergence speed, and initialization-dependent propagation timescales predict trainable sequence depth. This study is distinct from the listed CNN original, arXiv:1806.05393.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that signal-propagation theory predicts recurrent trainability, critical initialization improves training dynamics, and gating substantially broadens the trainable initialization region. Quantitative theory–experiment agreement weakens with tied weights.
record.recipe_differences: Tests recurrent networks on MNIST sequence tasks, rather than the feed-forward settings and CIFAR benchmarks in the claim versions; compares critical and off-critical initialization, including orthogonal and Gaussian weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization condition (critical versus off-critical), RNN architecture (vanilla versus minimalRNN), sequence depth, and weight tying affect training outcomes or agreement with the theoretical timescale.

fits_no_version.finding: Critical initialization improves gated minimalRNN training, and off-critical minimalRNNs fail at T=784.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization that preserves signal propagation improves convergence and sequence trainability in gated recurrent networks.

fits_no_version.finding: MinimalRNNs retain long-sequence trainability across a broader initialization region than vanilla RNNs, despite receiving one tenth as many training steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gating broadens the initialization region permitting long-sequence training.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization has insignificant influence on minimalRNN training speed; the well-conditioned minimalRNN trains three times faster than vanilla RNN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gating changes the role of weight orthogonality in trainability and can accelerate recurrent training.

record.problems: The main trainability comparisons are reported in figures; individual outcomes for Figure 2 are not numerically stated in the text. The experiments use MNIST-derived sequence tasks, not CIFAR classification. Text reports quantitative deviations between theory and experiments for tied weights.
record.rows_left_out: None. Figure 2 sweep results are included as figure-only rows because the text reports the setup and qualitative tied/untied comparison but not individual plotted values.

untested.parts: Convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/100, including random labels and size or regularization effects.
Teacher–student ReLU networks, spurious minima, and extra student neurons.
Depth degradation in plain convolutional networks, residual shortcuts, and Fixup.
Feedforward and convolutional training, comparisons across activation functions, and training 10,000-layer convolutional networks. Recurrent sequence length supplies the tested depth analogue.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, sharpness evolution, and divergence.
Batch-normalization speed and learning-rate comparisons, including Fixup alternatives.

missing.what: Separate vanilla-RNN orthogonal-versus-Gaussian training-speed comparisons under matched criticality. The text explicitly reports a significant speed difference; existing rows capture only critical versus off-critical initialization.
Successful critically initialized vanilla-RNN training at T=784, separated by weight distribution where readable, to complete the comparator for R4.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied title and arXiv:1806.05394 identify the RNN paper; arXiv:1806.05393 is the distinct CNN original. Tied-weight errors qualify the theory's numerical predictions, not V4's qualitative initialization claim. Figure graphics are unavailable in the supplied text, so no individual plotted values are inferred.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification, random or corrupted labels, and model size, early stopping, or regularization effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and spurious local minima.
Plain versus residual convolutional networks and shortcut effects; training without normalization using Fixup.
Feed-forward networks, activation-matched initializations, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks. The paper tests recurrent networks on MNIST sequence tasks.
Learning rates above stability thresholds, loss increases, curvature or sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization comparisons, CIFAR-10 or ImageNet experiments, and Fixup.

rows.subject: Vanilla RNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a sequence task built from MNIST with depth T=196 under critical orthogonal initialization.
rows.baseline: Vanilla RNN with off-critical initialization took over 16,000 updates to reach 90% test accuracy.
rows.value: Reached 90% test accuracy after 750 optimization steps.
rows.note: The paper says the critical versus off-critical speed difference for vanilla RNNs was two orders of magnitude.
rows.check: The numerical comparison is correct. Describe 16,000 versus 750 updates as over 21-fold; the authors' two-orders-of-magnitude description overstates this particular numerical comparison. The prose does not explicitly assign both counts to a particular weight distribution.
